subject: physics
question_text: Explain the concept of absolute zero of temperature on the basis of kinetic theory.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 13 Short Answer Question 3 (printed p.139). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: ½mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT falls to zero only at T = 0 on the absolute scale, and P = ⅔(E/V) means the pressure of an ideal gas falls to zero too; absolute zero is this theoretical limit, never reached by any real gas because every real gas liquefies first.

where T is the absolute temperature.
steps.margin_note: State the relation between average kinetic energy and T before discussing the limit.
steps.why: This relation is the only place T appears in the kinetic picture of a gas, so its behaviour as T falls decides what absolute zero means.
common_mistakes: Starting from the ideal gas equation PV = Nk_BT instead. The energy relation connects directly to molecular motion, which this question asks about.
steps.memory_tip: Average kinetic energy and absolute temperature: one relation, ½mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT.

steps.label: The zero point
lines: As T decreases, the average kinetic
energy ½mv̄² decreases in direct
proportion.
It can fall to zero only when T = 0
on the absolute (kelvin) scale.
steps.margin_note: Say clearly that T = 0 is where the average kinetic energy becomes zero.
steps.why: Since ½mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT is a direct proportion with no additive constant, the only temperature at which the average kinetic energy is zero is T = 0 itself.
common_mistakes: Saying molecular motion slows down at absolute zero. Kinetic theory says it stops completely — the average kinetic energy is exactly zero.
steps.memory_tip: Zero kinetic energy needs zero T — a direct proportion has no other zero.

steps.label: Pressure at T = 0
lines: Since pressure is related to the
translational kinetic energy by
the pressure of an ideal gas would
also fall to zero at T = 0.
steps.margin_note: Connect the falling kinetic energy to the falling pressure of the gas.
steps.why: P = ⅔(E/V) makes pressure directly proportional to the total translational kinetic energy E, so the same zero at T = 0 carries through to the pressure of an ideal gas.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the falling kinetic energy without connecting it to a falling pressure — the question is about the gas's observable behaviour too.
steps.memory_tip: Zero average kinetic energy means zero pressure too, through P = ⅔(E/V).

steps.label: The definition and its limit
lines: Absolute zero is the temperature at
which molecular translational
motion, and so the pressure of an
ideal gas, would fall to zero.
It is a theoretical limit. No real
gas reaches it, because every real
gas liquefies before T = 0 is
reached.
steps.margin_note: State both the definition AND that it is a limit no real gas reaches.
steps.why: The definition follows directly from the previous two steps, and the liquefaction point matters because kinetic theory assumes molecules interact only through elastic collisions — an assumption that fails once a real gas condenses.
common_mistakes: Saying absolute zero has been reached in real experiments. Only temperatures a small fraction of a kelvin above it have been reached; every real gas liquefies first.
steps.memory_tip: Absolute zero is a limit approached, never reached — real gases liquefy first.

insider_note: The mark for stating that no real gas reaches absolute zero, because every real gas liquefies first, is often missed — students give the definition and stop.
